source.title_on_document: Generative AI as an External Cognitive Tool for Developing Creative Intelligence in Visual Design: A Mixed-Methods Randomized Study Using Cognitive Load Indicators and Motivational Modeling

supplement.where: No supplementary material or online appendix is mentioned. Data Availability Statement (p. 28): 'Data are contained within the article.' The word 'supplementary' on p. 20 (Table 12) refers to an in-text table of indirect effects, not a supplement.

paper_design_summary: 120 second-year visual communication design undergraduates were randomly assigned at the individual level (60/60) to a six-week illustration course taught either as a GenAI-integrated, design-thinking course (ChatGPT, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Runway at each stage) or as a traditional course in which GenAI was used only sporadically; the two groups were taught in separate classes. Six experts rated the 24 final group projects (12 per arm) on five dimensions (creativity, applicability, technicality, expressiveness, completeness) on a 100-point scale, and students answered an end-of-course questionnaire on cognitive load, ARCS motivation, and perceived teaching alignment that was analyzed with PLS-SEM.

studies.label: Six-week illustration design course experiment (GenAI-integrated vs traditional instruction)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Course section: GenAI-integrated design-thinking instruction (experimental) vs traditional illustration instruction with only sporadic GenAI use (control). The two groups were taught in separate classes.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned at the individual level into an experimental group and a control group, with 60 students in each group, and the two groups were taught in separate classes.

arms.name: Experimental (GenAI-integrated instruction)
arms.description: Integrated teaching model: GenAI embedded in all five design-thinking stages (Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test) as a 'task chain + tool chain'; workshop-based, group collaboration and iterative cycles (Figure 2, p. 7; Table 2, p. 11).

arms.name: Control (traditional instruction)
arms.description: Traditional illustration teaching; 'GenAI tools are used sporadically (e.g., sketch generation, style reference); manual drawing and conventional digital software remain dominant' (Table 2, p. 11); lecturer-led instruction and independent assignments.

participants.exclusions: None reported. Questionnaire analysis uses n = 60 per group (Table 7, p. 15) and n = 120 at the student level (p. 20). The expert-rated outcome is analyzed at the project level: 24 group projects (p. 12, p. 20); the paper does not state team size or whether every student belonged to a rated project.
participants.who: Second-year undergraduates majoring in Visual Communication Design, same major and cohort, enrolled in the Illustration Design course in the same semester, volunteers
participants.country: not_stated (site called 'College X'; authors and approving IRB at Hanyang University, Seoul, Republic of Korea)
participants.quote: All participants were second-year students from the same major and cohort who were enrolled in the Illustration Design course during the same semester and voluntarily participated in the study.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Runway, and unnamed AIGC tools (Figure 2); model versions not stated
ai_tool.how_used: Experimental group used GenAI at every course stage: ChatGPT and Midjourney for user profiles and scene contexts (week 1), ChatGPT and Stable Diffusion for keyword clustering and problem statements (week 2), Midjourney and Stable Diffusion for divergent idea sketches (week 3), AIGC-assisted illustration generation and layout (week 4), Runway and AI for feedback analysis (week 5) (Figure 2, p. 7). Control group used GenAI only sporadically during sketching or material preparation (p. 10).

task.description: Illustration design course structured on design thinking; outcome is the final group illustration/design project (final images, brief design statement, key process summary), rated by experts.
task.duration: Six weeks; identical teaching weeks, in-class hours, assignment windows, and deadline in both arms (p. 12)

outcomes.name: Overall expert evaluation score (mean of five dimensions)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Six experts with teaching and industry experience in illustration and visual communication rated anonymized final group projects in a randomized order on a 100-point scale; project score = mean of five dimensions (creativity, applicability, technicality, expressiveness, completeness) (pp. 11-12, Table 3). The paper says discrepancies were 'resolved through iterative discussion until consensus was reached' (p. 20) yet also reports ICC(2,1) = 0.670 and ICC(2,k) = 0.924, 95% CI [0.847, 0.947] (p. 22, Table 14). Composite of design quality that includes but is not limited to creativity; the abstract calls it 'expert-rated creative performance'.

contrasts.reported: Independent-sample t-test at the project level (n = 24): experimental M = 86.58, SD = 1.84 vs control M = 79.94, SD = 2.98; t(22) = 6.57, p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 2.68. Per-project scores in Table 13 (12 Exp, 12 Ctrl).

outcomes.name: Creativity dimension (expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Dimension labeled 'Creativity'; evaluation focus 'Novelty of concept and visual expression'; 'Evaluates the uniqueness and degree of innovation in conceptual thinking, narrative logic, and visual language' (Table 3, p. 12). Six experts, 100-point scale.

contrasts.reported: No arm-level mean, SD, or test printed for this dimension. Table 13 lists each project's Creativity mean (Exp W01-W12: 88.50, 87.50, 89.00, 86.33, 88.33, 87.00, 89.33, 87.67, 89.83, 82.17, 88.33, 89.17; Ctrl W13-W24: 80.00, 73.50, 74.67, 84.50, 81.00, 81.50, 85.33, 76.67, 83.83, 77.67, 80.17, 78.50). Figure 6 boxplot; text: experimental group 'has higher median scores than the control group across all dimensions'.
contrasts.locator: p. 21, Table 13; p. 22, Figure 6; p. 21 text

company_involvement.description: Funding: 'This research received no external funding.' Conflicts of interest: none declared.

eligibility.reason: Individual-level random assignment of 120 students (60/60) to GenAI-integrated instruction vs traditional instruction with only sporadic GenAI use (p. 9); experts rated the creativity of the final outputs (pp. 11-12, 20-21). Caveats: the outcome is scored on 24 group projects, not on individuals, and team size is not stated; each arm was taught as one separate class, so arm is confounded with class; the treatment bundles GenAI with design-thinking pedagogy; the control arm also used GenAI sporadically, so the contrast is a different AI configuration rather than no AI.

one_line_finding: Final group projects from the GenAI-integrated course received higher expert scores than those from the traditional course (M = 86.58, SD = 1.84 vs 79.94, SD = 2.98; t(22) = 6.57, p < 0.001; d = 2.68 over 24 projects; p. 20), and higher medians on every dimension including creativity (Table 13, Figure 6).
open_questions: Comparison type: coded ai_design because the control arm used GenAI sporadically (Table 2, p. 11; p. 10); it could instead be treated as ai_vs_bau given the paper's 'traditional instruction' label.
The treatment bundles GenAI with a design-thinking, workshop-based, group-collaboration pedagogy (Table 2), so the contrast is not AI alone.
Arms were taught in two separate classes (p. 9): treatment is confounded with class at the level that matters for clustering.
Outcome unit is the group project (24 total, 12 per arm); team size and team formation are not reported. Whether n = 120 people or n = 24 teams should count for criterion 2 needs a decision.

Creativity dimension coded as novelty (its stated focus is 'Novelty of concept and visual expression'); the overall score is a five-dimension design-quality composite coded as other. Either could be argued as overall_creativity.

Expert-rating procedure is internally inconsistent: experts 'independently evaluated' works, discrepancies were 'resolved through iterative discussion until consensus was reached' (p. 20), yet ICCs across six raters are reported (p. 22).
notes: Questionnaire outcomes (intrinsic, extraneous, germane load; attention, relevance, confidence, satisfaction; integrated teaching alignment) are self-reports on a five-point Likert scale collected at the end of the course (Table 4, p. 13; Table 7, p. 15; PLS-SEM and MGA in Tables 8-12) and are not listed as outcomes. Baseline design-task score (Table 1, p. 10: control 74.6 +/- 6.8, experimental 75.4 +/- 7.1, rated by two course instructors) is a pretest, not an outcome. Structured interviews with 2 lecturers and 10 experimental-group students (p. 13) are qualitative. IRB approval: Hanyang University, 22 August 2025 (p. 28). Control group received the integrated course content after the experiment (p. 11).
